title: The Full Humanity of Christ

keyTerms.d: The eternal Son of God, without ceasing to be God, took to himself a complete human nature — body and rational soul — and was born, lived, and died as a genuine human being. Without ceasing to be God rules out the idea that the deity was traded away for the humanity; complete human nature rules out a Christ who is human on the outside only; born, lived, and died insists this is history, not appearance.

It is the eternal Son — the second person of the Trinity — who assumed a human nature, adding humanity to his deity. Not that the Father or the divine nature turned into flesh, nor that God suffered as God: the divine nature did not convert into a human one; the Son took humanity to himself while remaining fully, unchangeably God.

The historic confession is not either God or man, and not a blend of the two into something that is neither; it is the harder, stranger claim that he is fully God and fully man. Two full natures, one person — neither absorbed into the other, neither diminished by the other.

The boundary that has defined orthodox Christianity across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant lines ever since: one and the same Christ, “truly God and truly man,” “consubstantial with us according to the manhood; in all things like unto us, without sin,” made known in two natures without confusion, change, division, or separation.

From the Greek dokein, “to seem”: the view that Christ only appeared to have a body and only seemed to suffer — the very error 1 John was written against. If Christ’s suffering was theater, then so was our salvation.

Apollinaris of Laodicea granted Christ a human body but taught that the divine Word simply replaced the human mind or soul; the church condemned the view at the Council of Constantinople in 381. It sounds pious and seems to protect the deity, but it leaves Christ’s humanity a shell.

keyTerms.t: “What is not assumed is not healed”
keyTerms.d: Gregory of Nazianzus’s reply to Apollinarianism: “that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved.” To save the whole person, the Son had to become a whole person.

Whether Christ was able to sin — posse non peccare (“able not to sin”) versus non posse peccare (“not able to sin”) — is a genuine intramural debate with serious defenders on each side. What all orthodox parties affirm is that his temptations were real and his sinlessness was actual.

derive.q: Paul never argues for Christ’s humanity; he everywhere assumes it — so as evidence, that is…?
derive.ans: a stronger kind of evidence, not a weaker one
derive.why: A thing presupposed offhandedly by a writer making some other point was not up for debate. And Paul’s letters, generally dated to the 50s of the first century, are the oldest datable Christian documents we possess — earlier than any of the Gospels.

derive.q: Romans 8:3 says “the likeness of sinful flesh,” not “the likeness of flesh” — so “likeness” bears on…?
derive.ans: “sinful,” not the reality of his flesh (on the widely defended reading)
derive.why: Christ took real, full human flesh, but not the sinfulness that marks fallen humanity. The point does not finally hinge on that grammatical judgment: even interpreters who construe the phrase differently agree on the two things the verse holds together — his flesh was genuine, and he was without sin.

derive.q: Christ can undo what Adam did — so he must stand…?
derive.ans: where Adam stood: as a real human being
derive.why: As one man’s trespass brought condemnation, so “the one man, Jesus Christ” brings the gift of grace; Christ is the head of a renewed humanity. But the typology does not reduce him to a merely human second Adam: the one who became the last Adam was already “in the form of God” before taking “the form of a servant” — a transition Adam never made.

derive.q: A high priest must belong to the people he represents — so the Son “had to be made like them”…?
derive.why: “Since the children have flesh and blood, he too shared in their humanity” (Hebrews 2:14, 17). The logic is that of representation. And it presses toward comfort: he “has been tempted in every way, just as we are — yet he did not sin” (Hebrews 4:15). His temptations were real; his sinlessness was real.

derive.q: If the Son did not take a human mind, what is left unredeemed?
derive.ans: the human mind — the very seat of our rebellion
derive.why: Gregory of Nazianzus: “that which He has not assumed He has not healed.” To save the whole person, the Son had to become a whole person — full humanity, assumed by one who was already fully God.

derive.q: Grant all of it: the sources present a genuinely human Jesus. Does that, by itself, prove his deity?
derive.ans: no — it establishes the humanity; the deity is argued separately, and the faith confesses both
derive.why: This does not by itself prove the deity of Christ — that case is made elsewhere, and it must be. Nor does it resolve every mystery in how one person can be at once infinite and finite; the creeds fenced that mystery rather than dissolving it. What it establishes is modest and immovable: a genuinely human Jesus, affirmed alongside, never instead of, his full deity.

honestState.p1: On the main claim, the picture is far less contested than the surrounding footnotes might suggest. That Jesus was a real first-century human being is common ground between confessing Christians and the great majority of secular historians; scholars who deny his deity almost all still affirm his humanity. The live scholarly debate is almost entirely about the other nature — how early, and how high, the confession of his deity runs.
honestState.fairness: Two places where thoughtful, orthodox Christians disagree, and on which this argument takes no side: whether Christ was able to sin (his real temptation and actual sinlessness are affirmed; the further question is not settled here), and the relation of Jesus’ brothers to Mary, a Marian question that has long divided Catholic and Orthodox Christians from Protestants — the argument rests only on the plain fact that the earliest sources speak of Jesus’ human family. And the authorship of the Pastoral Epistles is disputed in critical scholarship; the case stands complete without them.
honestState.verdict: The earliest and best sources present Jesus as a genuine human being — born of a woman, living under the law, taking real flesh, tempted, bleeding, dying — and the church has always confessed exactly that, over against every attempt to make him merely seem human. The Incarnation is not God wearing humanity like a garment he might slip off; it is the eternal Son making our nature his own, all the way down to the grave, so that what he assumed he might heal. A Christ who is not one of us cannot represent us, cannot die for us, and cannot sympathize with us. The gospel needs him to be, and joyfully confesses him to be, fully God and fully man.

order: The earliest sources present Jesus as a genuine human being.
The same sources give him the worship and divine name reserved for God alone — so the humanity does not compete with the deity.
Therefore Jesus is fully God and fully man — two full natures in one person.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and what it does not say.
cards.a: The earliest and best sources present Jesus as a genuine human being: “born of a woman” (Galatians 4:4), sent “in the likeness of sinful flesh” yet without sin (Romans 8:3), “the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5), “made like them, fully human in every way” (Hebrews 2:17). Not that Jesus was a mere man: the one who is God also became truly man.

The same sources give Jesus the worship and the divine name reserved for God alone — so the humanity does not compete with the deity. The church confessed both together against Docetism and Apollinarianism, and sealed it at Chalcedon: truly God and truly man.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That Jesus is fully God and fully man — two full natures in one person — and that only such a Christ can represent us, truly die for us, and sympathize with us. It does not by itself prove the deity (that case is made elsewhere; the faith confesses both natures together), nor dissolve the mystery of one person at once infinite and finite.

cards.q: Why is Paul’s assuming the humanity, rather than arguing it, strong evidence?
cards.a: Because a thing presupposed offhandedly by a writer making some other point was not up for debate. And it comes from the oldest datable Christian documents we possess, earlier than any of the Gospels.

cards.q: “Born of a woman, born under the law” — what does each phrase establish?
cards.a: Born of a woman: the Son entered the world through a mother, in a body. Born under the law: he entered it as a first-century Jew, bound by Torah, located in a real people at a real moment. It is the Son who entered the world this way — without ceasing to be God.

cards.q: What does the last-Adam typology establish — and what does it not?
cards.a: It establishes real humanity: Christ can undo what Adam did only because he stands where Adam stood, as a real human being. It does not reduce him to a merely human second Adam: the one who became the last Adam was already “in the form of God” before taking a servant’s form — a transition Adam never made.

cards.q: Why, by Hebrews’ logic, must the Son be fully human?
cards.a: The logic is that of representation: a high priest must belong to the people he represents. So he “had to be made like them, fully human in every way,” in order to become a merciful and faithful high priest — tempted in every way, just as we are, yet without sin.

cards.q: Name the three things that hang on the full humanity.
cards.a: Representation — a savior who was not truly one of us could not truly stand in for us. A real death — only what is genuinely human can genuinely die. Sympathy — he understands our weaknesses from the inside, as one who has been here. What is not assumed is not healed.

cards.q: What did Docetism hold — and why was it a gospel matter, not a quibble?
cards.a: That Christ only appeared to have a body and only seemed to suffer — the error 1 John was written against, where the flesh became the test. A phantom cannot bleed, and a phantom’s cross saves no one: if Christ’s suffering was theater, then so was our salvation.

cards.q: What did Apollinarianism hold — and what principle answers it?
cards.a: That the divine Word simply replaced Christ’s human mind or soul. It sounds pious, but it leaves his humanity a shell. The answer: what is not assumed is not healed — if the Son did not take a human mind, the human mind is left unredeemed; to save the whole person, the Son had to become a whole person.

One and the same Christ, truly God and truly man, like us in all things without sin, made known in two natures without confusion, change, division, or separation. Two full natures, one person — neither absorbed into the other, neither diminished by the other.

cards.q: Reply to: “The man Christ Jesus” is from the disputed Pastorals, so drop it.
cards.a: Concede the disputed authorship; nothing in the case depends on it. Galatians 4:4, Romans 8:3, 1 Corinthians 15, and the humanity of the Philippians hymn are in the undisputed letters, and Hebrews and the Gospels stand outside the Pastorals question. Remove them and the case is unweakened.

obj.q: So much human evidence — born, tempted, ignorant of the hour, dying. You have described a man: a human being whom later Christians promoted to divinity.
obj.model: Grant the concession first: the human evidence is pervasive and real — that is the whole point of the doctrine. What does not follow is that humanity competes with deity. The same early sources that show Jesus hungry also give him the worship and divine name reserved for YHWH alone. The disagreement is not really about dates — Ehrman himself finds a pre-existent Christ in material older than Paul’s letters — but about what kind of being the earliest Christians took him to be; and the earliest evidence answers it: Marana tha (1 Corinthians 16:22), Aramaic prayer addressed to him by the first Judean church. As for Mark 13:32, the orthodox tradition has long held that the Son’s not knowing the hour belongs to the genuine limits of his human consciousness, not to a deficiency in the divine nature he never ceased to possess. The right conclusion from the abundant humanity is not “therefore only a man,” but “therefore truly a man.” So the developmental objection does not hold.

obj.q: Romans 8:3 says Christ came in the “likeness” of sinful flesh — likeness, not the thing itself. So Paul is hedging: Jesus only resembled a human being.
obj.model: The phrase is “the likeness of sinful flesh,” not “the likeness of flesh.” On a reading widely defended in the commentary tradition, the qualifier bears on “sinful,” not on the reality of his flesh: Christ took real, full human flesh, but not the sinfulness that marks fallen humanity. And the point does not finally hinge on the grammar — interpreters who construe it differently still agree on the two things the verse holds together: his flesh was genuine, and he was without sin.

obj.q: One person cannot be both infinite and finite, all-knowing and growing in wisdom. “Fully God and fully man” is a form of words papering over a contradiction.
obj.model: The confession does not say one nature is both — it says one person subsists in two distinct natures, “without confusion” and “without change,” so that no property of one nature cancels the other. That is not shown to be contradictory; it is a mystery. Honesty requires admitting the creeds fenced the mystery of how one person can be at once infinite and finite rather than dissolving it — but “hard to picture” is not the same as “incoherent,” and the objection has to show both sets of properties predicated of one nature in the same respect, which is exactly what Chalcedon denies.

obj.q: Hebrews says he was “tempted in every way, just as we are.” Temptation is only real if failing is possible — so either it was play-acting, or he could have sinned, which God cannot.
obj.model: What every orthodox Christian affirms, and all this argument affirms, is that his temptations were real and his sinlessness was actual — the two are held together, not played against each other (Hebrews 4:15). Whether he was able to sin — the old distinction between “able not to sin” and “not able to sin” — is a genuine intramural debate with serious defenders on each side, and this is deliberately not the place it is settled. The objection assumes one answer to that in-house question; it does not touch the shared claim that the temptation and the sinlessness were both real.

unseen.q: A full doctrine of the incarnation emerges clearly only in John’s Gospel. Paul’s Son is a man God exalted — or, as adoptionists held, adopted — nowhere a prior being who became anything.
unseen.model: “Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9) reads most naturally — though a metaphor of earthly poverty is possible — as a transition from a prior state. And adoptionism founders on the same texts: Paul’s Son is sent “when the set time had fully come,” not created or adopted en route; he is the one who was “in the form of God” before he took a servant’s form — a transition Adam never made. The pre-existence question is a real and ongoing scholarly debate, not a settled rout, though the weight of recent scholarship has moved toward reading genuine pre-existence in the text. The development is in the clarity, not in the substance: full humanity, assumed by one who was already fully God.
